Planning a whole-house renovation in Vancouver in 2026 means navigating real costs, BC Building Code timelines, and contractor availability that most articles skip. This guide gives you the sequential process with actual dollar figures so you know exactly where your money goes.

Step 1: Confirm You Actually Need a Whole-House Renovation ($800-$1,500 for Assessment)

Before signing any contract, hire a renovation consultant or independent inspector to assess what work is truly required. This is not the same as a real-estate inspection -- it costs $800-$1,500 depending on home size and covers structural integrity, electrical panel capacity, plumbing pipe material (Poly-B, galvanized, or copper), insulation levels, and HVAC adequacy. Reno Stars includes this assessment as part of our initial consultation at no additional charge.

A common mistake in Vancouver is assuming cosmetic updates solve underlying problems. If your home has Poly-B plumbing (homes built 1975-1995), any whole-house scope should budget $15,000-$35,000 for re-piping -- a cost that appears mid-project when it should be in the opening budget. Similarly, knob-and-tube wiring, present in many pre-1960 homes, requires full replacement at $15,000-$40,000 before walls can be opened.

Step 2: Define Your Renovation Tier -- Budget Determines Scope

Whole-house renovations in Vancouver fall into four cost tiers, each with a distinct scope and timeline:

  • Cosmetic Refresh: $49,000-$80,000. Flooring, trim, interior painting, kitchen and bathroom fixture updates. No structural or mechanical work. 4-6 months total.
  • Mid-Range Whole-House: $80,000-$150,000. One kitchen gut, two bathroom gut-rehabs, retextured walls, new lighting throughout, partial rewire. 6-9 months.
  • Substantial Renovation: $150,000-$250,000. Full kitchen and all bathrooms gutted, possible main-floor layout changes, new HVAC, full re-plumb, full rewire, new insulation. 9-15 months.
  • Structural Transformation: $250,000-$350,000+. Second-storey addition, foundation work, laneway house construction, significant structural modifications requiring an engineer. 15-30 months.

The 2025 median whole-house renovation cost in Greater Vancouver was $92,900 (RenovationFind, 2025). Most projects fall between $80,000-$150,000 for a livable transformation that addresses deferred maintenance and modernises the layout.

Step 3: Design and Pre-Construction (2-4 Months)

With a confirmed scope and budget, the design phase covers floor plans, material selections, and contractor pricing. Architects in Vancouver charge $75-$175 per hour, with flat-fee whole-house design ranging $8,000-$25,000 depending on complexity. Reno Stars provides in-house design services that eliminate the architect markup for most whole-house projects.

Pre-construction includes applying for building permits. In Vancouver, a whole-house renovation permit typically takes 4-8 weeks for routine work; projects involving structural changes or additions can take 12-20 weeks due to required engineering reviews. BC Building Code Division C, Section 3.7 requires an energy efficiency upgrade report for any renovation exceeding 75% of the home's wall, floor, and ceiling surfaces -- a requirement that adds 2-4 weeks and $2,000-$5,000 to the permit package.

Step 4: Hiring Your Contractor -- What Vancouver Contracts Must Include

Vancouver homeowners have specific legal protections under the Home Improvement Act. Your contract must include: the contractor's Consumer Protection BC license number, a detailed scope of work with material specifications, an itemized price breakdown, a start date and substantial completion date, a 10% holdback clause (legally required), and the contractor's WSBC clearance letter confirming they carry workers' compensation coverage.

Red flags that should end a conversation: a contractor asking for more than 10% deposit, refusing to provide a written contract, offering a price if you sign today, or lacking a WSBC account. Reno Stars holds full WSBC coverage and provides license documentation upfront -- ask for it before the first meeting ends. For whole-house projects, always request a fixed-price contract rather than a time-and-materials arrangement.

Step 5: Construction Phase -- What Happens When

A typical whole-house renovation sequence follows this order, regardless of contractor:

  • Weeks 1-2: Demolition and hazardous material abatement. Asbestos testing and removal ($8,000-$40,000 if present in vermiculite insulation or old floor tiles) happens before general demo begins.
  • Weeks 3-4: Structural repairs, framing changes, and engineering inspections. No finishes begin until the structural package passes inspection.
  • Weeks 5-8: Mechanical rough-ins -- electrical, plumbing, HVAC. This is the phase most likely to reveal Poly-B or knob-and-tube issues requiring budget adjustments.
  • Weeks 9-12: Insulation, vapour barrier, and drywall. Building code requires R-22 minimum for attics and R-12 for exterior walls in Vancouver's Climate Zone 4.
  • Weeks 13-16: Finishes -- tiling, flooring, cabinetry, painting, fixture installation. This phase moves quickly when materials have been pre-ordered and confirmed on-site.
  • Weeks 17-20: Final electrical and plumbing trim, HVAC commissioning, and city final inspection.

Timeline adjustments of 2-4 weeks are normal for Vancouver weather delays (October-March rain affects exterior work) and for material supply chains that remain unpredictable in 2026.

Step 6: Budget Contingency -- The Line Item Most Homeowners Skip

BC renovation professionals consistently recommend a contingency fund separate from your base contract. For pre-1970 homes, budget 15% contingency. For homes built after 1990, 10% is sufficient. A home built between 1975-1990 with Poly-B plumbing should carry 20% contingency given the likelihood of hidden pipe replacement.

Common surprises in Vancouver whole-house projects: rotted subfloor discovered after flooring removal, moisture damage behind shower walls requiring re-framing, undersized electrical panels when adding new circuits, and HVAC units at end-of-life when the existing furnace is inspected mid-project.

Step 7: Final Walkthrough, Holdback Release, and Warranty

BC law requires a 5-day cooling-off period after signing a home renovation contract. After work is substantially complete, the provincial requirement is a mandatory 10% holdback retained for 6 months after completion to cover any deficiencies.

Before releasing final payment, conduct a written punch-list walkthrough with your contractor. Document everything -- a light switch that does not operate, paint scuffs, caulking gaps. Whole-House Renovation FAQs

How long does a whole-house renovation take in Vancouver in 2026?

A cosmetic refresh takes 4-6 months from permit to keys. A mid-range whole-house project runs 6-9 months. Substantial renovations requiring layout changes or mechanical upgrades take 9-15 months. Structural transformations including additions or second-storey work take 15-30 months.

What is the average cost per square foot for a whole-house renovation in Vancouver?

In 2025-2026, whole-house renovation costs in Greater Vancouver average $140-$200 per square foot for mid-range work, not including land value or permit fees. A 2,000 sq ft home renovated to mid-range standards typically costs $280,000-$400,000. This figure varies significantly based on scope, age of home, and whether structural or mechanical systems require replacement.

Do I need a building permit for a whole-house renovation in Vancouver?

Yes. Any renovation altering structure, changing the use or occupancy of a room, adding or removing walls, or modifying plumbing or electrical systems requires a building permit. Cosmetic work such as painting, replacing flooring, and installing new fixtures without altering rough-ins typically does not require a permit. BC Building Code requires structural permits for any wall removal or header installation.

How do I budget for a whole-house renovation if my home has Poly-B pipes?

Poly-B piping was installed in approximately 60% of Vancouver-area homes built between 1975-1995. A whole-house renovation scope should include a plumbing assessment before pricing. Poly-B re-piping costs $15,000-$35,000 depending on the number of fixtures and whether the runs are accessible (basement) or require wall opening. Reno Stars includes a plumbing assessment in our initial consultation.

What percentage of a whole-house renovation budget goes to the kitchen?

The kitchen typically consumes 30-40% of a mid-range whole-house renovation budget. A complete kitchen gut-rehab with new cabinetry, quartz countertops, quality appliances, and proper lighting runs $45,000-$75,000 in Vancouver. Each additional full bathroom gut-rehab adds $15,000-$27,000 to the budget.
